title: A hymn in Tukhari
hookLine: Tukhari holds Guru Nanak's own twelve months

cards: Which month is it where you are? Guru Nanak has a verse for it. A year turns like a wall calendar, each page with its own picture: blossoms, then a hot sun, then rain clouds, then frost.

Raga Tukhari holds his Barah Maha, the twelve months, and it walks the whole year, page by page, with a soul longing for its Beloved. Back on day 564 you met Guru Arjan's twelve months in Majh. This one is Guru Nanak's.

teach.b: The poem opens before any month begins, with a call to listen: our lives are shaped by what we've done, and the soul, like a bride, can't find joy apart from the Beloved. Then the calendar turns. Chet comes first.
In plain English, not word for word: Chet is lovely, it's spring, and the bumblebees are beautiful. The forest blooms. And still, the bride says, without the Beloved at home, how can there be peace?
A hot month comes, with a scorching sun. The rains come in Savan, and the bride says her mind and body love her Husband Lord.
Then the frost of Poh, and on to the end of the year. Every season gets its weather and its longing. Here's the turn at the end.

teach.h: EVERY MONTH BLESSED WHEN THE ONE COMES.
teach.b: Once the Beloved is met, the poem looks back over everything: the twelve months, the seasons, the days, the hours, the moments, all of them are blessed when the True One comes. The calendar didn't change. The bride did.
The Granth's other Barah Maha, Guru Arjan's in Majh, is read in some gurdwaras when a new month begins. But this one is Guru Nanak's own. It doesn't ask for a better season.
It asks for the Beloved, and then every season is good.

how: Guru Nanak's Barah Maha is sung in Raga Tukhari in kirtan. Guru Arjan's Barah Maha in Raga Majh is read in some gurdwaras at the start of each month of the Indian calendar.

games.q: what does “a hymn in tukhari” mean?
o: a set of hymns for the twelve hours of day and night
a list of the festival days marked through the Sikh year
Guru Nanak's poem walking the twelve months with a longing soul

games.q: what's inside the hymn — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak's poem asks for a better season
it asks for the Beloved; once the True One comes, every month is blessed.
the Granth holds more than one Barah Maha
Guru Nanak's is in Tukhari; Guru Arjan's is in Raga Majh.
the poem begins straight away with the first month
it opens with a call to listen before Chet begins.

games.q: you're the bride at the end of Nanak's year. the Beloved has come. what happens to the months behind you?
o: only spring is remembered as good.
all of them are called blessed.
games.why: the last verse blesses the twelve months, the seasons, the days and the moments, once the True One comes. the calendar didn't change; the bride did.

practice: Start with this month: what's the weather outside right now?
Feel it for a breath, then let your mind move back a season, and another, the way Guru Nanak's poem moves page by page, finding in each one moment you were glad, however small.
If you pray, say Waheguru at each season you pass; if you don't, simply name the moment to yourself.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Tukhari. Guru Nanak's Barah Maha, the twelve months, which walks the year with a longing soul and ends with every season blessed. Today's word.

orig.note: barah maha, the twelve months: the name of Guru Nanak's poem in Raga Tukhari.

carryVoice: Your line: Nanak's months. Once the Beloved comes, every month in the poem is blessed. Go gently.
